bolp.etymology: From Latin vulpēs, vulpem. Compare Friulian bolp, Romansh vulp, Venetan bolp, volp, bolpe, Dalmatian bualp, Istriot bulpo, Italian volpe.

uton.etymology: Borrowed from Latin autumnus (“autumn, fall”), of uncertain etymology. The Latin etymon is directly continued by Romanian toamnă, Aromanian toamnã (unless these reflect the variant in a-), Italian autono (Northern Italy, 15th c.), Romansh u

musciat.etymology: From Late Latin *muscella (“young mule”), probably via a Romance back-formation comparable to Friulian mus and Venetan muso.

tòch.etymology: Probably from Latin tucca (liquid lard).. Compare Italian tocco.

crëp.etymology: From a pre-Latin substrate *kripp- (“rock”). First attested in 1763 as craep, glossed with scopulus (“crag, cliff”).

nzaul.etymology: From Vulgar Latin unus non sapit unde (“one doesn't know where”).

fosch.etymology: From Latin fuscus. Compare Italian fosco, Spanish hosco, Portuguese fosco, fusco, Catalan fosc, Old French fusque.

lënia.etymology: From Latin ligna, plural of lignum.

lën.etymology: From Latin līgnum. Compare Friulian len, Italian legno.

marënda.etymology: From Latin merenda (“light evening meal”). Compare Romansh marenda, Venetan marenda, Italian merenda, all of which mean "afternoon snack".

scagn.etymology: From Latin scamnum. Compare Friulian scagn, Lombard scagn, Italian scanno.

isté.etymology: From Latin aestās, aestātem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ- (“burn; fire”).

biescia.etymology: From Late Latin, Vulgar Latin bīstia, from Latin bēstia. Cognate to Italian bestia and Italian biscia.

lënga.etymology: From Latin lingua, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s.

scintla.etymology: From German Schindel or Middle High German schindel, from Old High German scintula, from Proto-West Germanic *skindulā, from Late Latin scindula, from Latin scandula.
